##Revised Proposal 

My initial proposal was to replicate Bosker et al. (2014)'s paper on native and non-native disfluencies. However, after receiving valuable feedback and talking to Haoyu about the feasibility of the project, I decided to pursue another replication project that can fit better within the scope of the course. Due to the time constraints of having to replicate, collect data, and analyze the project within one quarter, I may not be able to create all the materials needed on time. For example, the study uses Dutch audio recordings and words while I would have to use English to be able to recruit participants. I would also need to match the frequency, target onset times, and reaction times for each English target. Additionally, the experiment's main findings were from eye-tracking rather than the reaction time. Below is my new proposal with a paper that does a behvaioral study and has open source materials to ensure better replication.


## Introduction

Recent research on language variability has demonstrated how different language environments shape language and cognitive processes. Specifically, Heritage bilinguals offer a powerful lens for understanding how becoming a dominant speaker in the second acquired language despite not having the first years of development in the language can provide insights into the plasticity of the language system. Therefore, understanding how language processing is shaped by the heritage bilingual experience and how that may differ from monolingual or second language learner is an important gap to address in the bilingualism literature. 

I am proposing a new project proposal, where I would like to further explore heritage speakers' abilities to comprehend relative clauses across varying syntactic complexity. Therefore, in order to test this, I will be replicating Fuchs and colleagues (2026)’s paper where they compared heritage speakers to English-raised bilinguals who are late bilinguals and learned Spanish only in the classroom setting and Spanish-raised bilinguals who were raised in Spanish-speaking dominant environment. They tested participants’ constraints when cognitive loading increased alongside syntactic complexity but also tested cognitive effort and syntactic complexity separately. For the purpose of this class, I will be replicating the experiment with heritage speakers in the picture-matching experiment which tested syntactic competence. The paper looked at three different types of sentences: Reduced Relative (RR), Subject Relative (SR), Object Relative (OR) in Spanish. RR tends to be the easiest condition as it follows a direct order of events for example “the bear painting the tiger.” SR on the other hand is when the subject becomes the actor so instead it is “the bear that is painting the tiger.” Finally, OR which is the most difficult syntactically as it starts with the noun where the sentence instead states “the bear that the tiger paints.” In this sentence, it is typically harder for people as they often initially assume the bear is the one enacting the painting and not the tiger but then have to revise their interpretation once they hear the full sentence. The key findings of this experiment is that  heritage speakers showed higher accuracy for Reduced Relatives than Subject Relatives (β = 0.87, SE = 0.22, z = 3.86, p < .001) and significantly higher accuracy for Subject Relatives than Object Relatives (β = 5.07, SE = 0.17, z = 29.52, p < .001), This means that heritage speakers tend to have difficulties in interpreting object relative clauses and show a relative-clause complexity effect. 


## Methods

To conduct this experiment, I will be implementing the experimental design from Fuchs and colleagues' (2026) design. Participants will hear a short Spanish phrase containing a relative clause and are instructed to select the picture that correctly matches the described event. Each trial will display two images depicting reversed agent-patient roles (e.g., a bear painting a tiger vs. a tiger painting a bear). The auditory stimuli will follow the structure of Article + Nouns + Relative Clause. As the task progresses, syntactic complexity will increase by using three types of relative clauses: Reduced Relatives, Subject Relative, and Object Relatives. All materials for this experiment has been provided through the OSF repository: https://osf.io/etprk/files/osfstorage?view_only=19f67921b4eb4ab58299685068ac0a16 along with analysis materials ensuring better replication of the experiment. 

The paper recruited 31 heritage Spanish speakers, who were born and raised in the U.S. or immigrated by age 6 and reported speaking Spanish with one or both parents. They also report English to be their most dominant language but having acquired Spanish since birth. Ensuring that I am recruiting the correct population and including the same criteria as the researchers will be the most important and challenging part of the project. This is because it will restrict the availability of people I can recruit from SONA but will be the most fitting to what the study tested. To do so, I will include similar language history questionnaires as the paper, the Bilingual Language Profile (BLP) and additional questions from  the Language Experience and Proficiency Questionnaire(LEAP-Q). Additionally, the organization and coding of the experiment on JavaScript will also be another learning challenge since participants completed 120 picture-matching trials so it is a substantive amount of images and audios to be coded. I would also like to extend this study by including variations of heritage speakers. The study categorized heritage speakers as those who report speaking Spanish with one or more parent and were born and raised in the U.S. or immigrated at the age of 6 or younger. All of the heritage speakers' report English dominance as they experience reduced Spanish input in an English dominant environment (U.S.). However, the study does not reveal variations within the heritage speakers' themselves and how those who more production experience may differ than those with limited production abilities but tends to be better at comprehension. This way I will be testing out to what extent does proficiency and immersion in the heritage language moderate the relative-clause complexity effect that the authors report for the heritage speakers. 


## Learning Goals

I am hoping through this project, to learn how to build a task through jsPsych that is well structured. I have not had much experience with building new tasks especially in jsPsych however as I progress in building my second year project for the cognitive science program, I will need to design and build new tasks to fit my project aims. I also want to learn implementing similar analysis and methods in a published paper in order to implement some type of replication within a new project. This will help ensure that I am following up and building on these results and testing whether these effects exist before beginning a whole new project. I believe this project will be feasible as all the materials have been provided but I will need to ensure that I am organizing the task correctly and starting participant recruitment early to ensure I have enough participants for analysis.  Additionally, this will be my first study looking at comprehension within bilinguals rather than production which will help inform my future projects towards assessing comprehension abilities and individual differences within heritage bilinguals.
